paras.text: Adjuster and Public Adjuster Licensing, Chapter Twelve of the Michigan Insurance Code: Audio Lecture

Welcome to Chapter Twelve. This is the domain that governs who may adjust an insurance claim in Michigan, who may charge a fee for helping a homeowner with a claim, and what happens to a contractor or public adjuster who steps over the line. It is the reason a restoration contractor cannot also be the person negotiating the claim, and the reason Jacob cannot hold a Michigan adjuster license while he is connected to a restoration company.

The big picture first. Chapter Twelve of the Insurance Code of nineteen fifty six, Act two eighteen, runs from M C L five hundred point twelve hundred through twelve forty seven. It licenses four kinds of people in one chapter: insurance producers, who you'd call agents, solicitors, adjusters, and insurance counselors, because all four touch an insurance transaction for pay.

Here is the first trap, and it is a big one. If you go looking for a definition of the word "adjuster," or the phrase "adjuster for the insured," which is Michigan's own term for what every other state calls a public adjuster, you will not find one. M C L five hundred point twelve zero one, the definitions section, defines agent, agent of the insured, agent of the insurer, insurance producer, negotiate, sell, and solicit. It does not define adjuster, adjuster for the insured, or independent adjuster. Those are operative words used throughout the chapter without ever being pinned down. DIFS's own paperwork stumbles on the same gap: in one of the cases we'll cover, DIFS pointed to two sections for the phrase "fire repair contractor," and those sections actually define "good moral character," not that phrase at all. So when you meet these terms, you are reconstructing their meaning from how they're used, not from a clean definition.

Now to the section that is the whole ballgame: M C L five hundred point twelve twenty two. Subsection one says a person shall not adjust loss or damage under a policy of insurance, or advertise, solicit business, or hold himself or herself out to the public as an adjuster, unless he or she is licensed as an adjuster. Notice there are three separate triggers packed into one sentence. Actually adjusting a loss is one. Advertising as an adjuster is a second. And just holding yourself out as one, even without a single claim file in hand, is a third. You do not have to touch a claim to violate this section. Offering the service is enough.

Subsection two lists the exemptions, and there are exactly five, lettered A through E. Memorize the count as hard as the content, because this is where exam writers and real-world contractors both love to insert a sixth that does not exist. Letter A, a person admitted to the practice of law in this state. Letter B, a marine average adjuster, a narrow maritime specialty. Letter C, an employee or manager of an authorized insurer adjusting a loss under a policy that same insurer issued. That's your everyday company adjuster, exempt because of the employment relationship, not a separate license. Letter D, a licensed insurance producer to whom the insurer has granted claim authority. Letter E, a narrow data-entry carve-out: someone who collects or furnishes claim information and enters it into a claims system, but only while supervised by a licensed independent adjuster or an exempt insurer employee. That's it. There is no contractor exemption anywhere in this list. A restoration contractor who writes an estimate, submits it to the carrier on the homeowner's behalf, and negotiates the settlement for a fee is doing exactly what this section licenses, and no relabeling changes that, unless that contractor is also a licensed Michigan attorney.

Next is M C L five hundred point twelve twenty four, which governs how you get the license. The commissioner decides a completed application within sixty days, may require a written exam, and can waive that exam for someone licensed as an adjuster within the preceding twelve months. Subsection three lists what the commissioner checks: reasonable understanding of the insurance being adjusted, reasonable understanding of Michigan insurance law, good faith intent, good business reputation, and good moral character.

But subsection four is the one this entire domain revolves around. Quote: the commissioner shall not issue a license to act as an adjuster to a person who is employed by, owns stock in, is an officer or director of, or in any other manner is connected with, a fire repair contractor. Four separate hooks in that sentence: employment, stock ownership, an officer or director title, or that broad catch-all, "in any other manner is connected with." This is a licensing bar, not a conduct standard. It stops the commissioner from ever issuing the license in the first place, before any misconduct is even alleged. This is exactly why Jacob cannot hold a Michigan adjuster license today. Any role with a restoration contractor, ownership, officer title, or that catch-all connection, closes the door before conduct ever comes into question.

Now the rules for the contract itself, in M C L five hundred point twelve twenty six. Four pieces. First, an adjuster for the insured cannot pay someone to help solicit or adjust a loss unless that person is both regularly employed by the adjuster and separately licensed. Second, when soliciting, the adjuster must orally identify as an adjuster for the insured and leave a card stating that title and their rates, and cannot claim to be an insurer's adjuster, a fire investigator, or connected to a fire department. Third, the number you must know cold: an adjuster for the insured shall not charge a rate exceeding ten percent of the amount paid by the insurer in settlement of the loss. DIFS's own guidance adds a wrinkle: that ten percent applies only to the coverages actually marked on the contract, so a public adjuster hired for building and contents cannot also take ten percent of a loss-of-use payment the contract never covered.

Fourth, and this is the piece that generates the most litigation: an adjuster for an insured shall not provide services to a client until there is a written contract, on a form approved by the commissioner, and a contract signed within forty eight hours of the loss is voidable at the insured's option for ten days after signing. A copy must be given to the insured at signing. Three separate requirements: the approved form, the forty-eight-hour and ten-day voidability window, and the copy requirement. Skip any one of them and you are exposed.

A companion conduct section, twelve twenty seven, adds three rules. No soliciting a loss while it is still happening or while fire department personnel are on scene. No collecting a fee from a repair contractor for steering repair work to that contractor, the statutory wall against adjuster-to-contractor kickbacks. And no advancing money to an insured while a claim is pending.

Now a different license entirely: insurance counselor, under M C L five hundred point twelve thirty two. It requires a license for anyone who audits or abstracts policies, or gives advice, counsel, or opinion about a policy's benefits, coverage, terms, or value. Here's the trap. The second sentence says a non-licensee shall not use terms such as consultant or consulting services, or any other language, in a way which implies that he or she is a licensed insurance counselor. Read that carefully: the word-ban is conditional on the implication of licensure. It is not an outright ban on the word "consultant" showing up anywhere near an insurance sentence. The much bigger exposure sits in the first sentence: writing a claim estimate "for every dollar owed" and submitting it to a carrier is advice about the value of the policy, and that is licensed territory regardless of what you call the fee. Attorneys are exempt from this section too, same as they are from the adjuster license requirement. A companion section, M C L five hundred point twelve thirty six, requires a signed written fee agreement in advance of any counselor service, retained for at least two years.

Now discipline and money, because these numbers get tested. M C L five hundred point twelve forty two is the procedural engine. The commissioner must give written notice with a hearing right before refusing a license, and may suspend or revoke after notice and a hearing for failing to maintain standards or violating the act. Subsection four is the emergency lever: without any prior hearing, the commissioner may summarily suspend a license if protection of the public requires emergency action. If a hearing is then requested, it must happen within twenty days, and a decision must be announced within thirty days after that hearing concludes.

M C L five hundred point twelve forty four is where the dollar amounts live. After a hearing, the director can order a civil fine of not more than one thousand dollars per violation, rising to not more than five thousand dollars per violation if the person knew or should have known they were violating the chapter, capped at fifty thousand dollars total per order. The director can also order a refund of overcharges, restitution to the insured, and suspension or revocation of the license. If someone then knowingly violates a resulting cease-and-desist order, the stakes go up again: up to twenty thousand dollars per violation, capped at one hundred thousand dollars per order.

Let's make all of this concrete with two real cases. The first is Aleksandr Guldshtadt, DIFS enforcement case number twenty five dash one eight three five zero. He was a licensed non-resident adjuster for the insured, affiliated with a firm called Nationwide Insurance Claims Advocates. DIFS summarily suspended his license on November third, twenty twenty five, under that emergency authority in twelve forty two, subsection four. His final decision came down April first, twenty twenty six: license revoked, and a fifty thousand dollar civil fine, sitting right at that statutory cap. What did DIFS find? He was listed as C E O of a California general contractor whose website advertised fire restoration, on that company's California corporate filings, and as its registered agent on the Michigan filings, even though he told a DIFS investigator he didn't partner with contractors. That's the "connected with a fire repair contractor" problem. Here is a precision point worth carrying into an exam. The categorical licensing bar in the statute is twelve twenty four, subsection four, but DIFS did not charge him under it. Because he was already licensed, DIFS ran the charge through twelve twenty four, subsection three, and twelve forty two, subsection two, failure to maintain the standards required for initial licensing. Know both routes: the text bar for an applicant, the maintenance route for a sitting licensee. He also entered more than twenty five public-adjusting contracts before DIFS ever approved his contract form, many of them carrying a thirty five percent fee, more than triple the ten percent cap. And he used unlicensed individuals to present those contracts to homeowners. One important detail: Guldshtadt never requested a hearing, so this whole decision rests on a default record, unchallenged allegations accepted as true, not findings tested in a contested hearing.

The second case is Tredenick versus Nationwide Agribusiness, involving a public adjuster called Prime Adjusting Service, Michigan Court of Appeals number three four nine eight eight seven, decided April eighth, twenty twenty one. This one is unpublished and per curiam, which means under the court rules it is persuasive only, not binding precedent, even though it is the clearest applied reading we have of that forty-eight-hour and ten-day rule. Here's what happened. After a farm fire, a licensed public adjuster signed an eight percent contract with the Tredenicks. The form Prime used was not a DIFS-approved form. It omitted the forty-eight-hour, ten-day voidability sentence, and it also lacked the Home Solicitation Sales Act three-day cancellation notice, though the Court of Appeals decided the case on the insurance-code defect alone. Watch the timing here, because it is the whole point: that contract was actually signed about a month after the fire, so the missing forty-eight-hour clause could not have helped these homeowners on these facts, and the court held that made no difference at all. The trial court let the Tredenicks void the contract, and denied the adjuster both its eight percent fee and a fallback claim for quantum meruit, which is payment for the reasonable value of services actually performed, even without an enforceable contract. The Court of Appeals affirmed both denials. Its key line is worth memorizing: given that the adjuster failed to meet the statutory condition precedent to perform public adjuster services, there is no inequity in denying it payment for those services. One small warning if you ever quote that line in writing: the opinion as published actually prints the word i n h e r i t, not inherent, so quote it exactly or paraphrase it, but never silently fix a court's text. Read the holding straight through. A licensed adjuster, on an eight percent contract, with a defective form, recovered nothing. Not the contract price, not a fallback payment. That is the baseline for measuring any percentage-fee claim by an unlicensed party on a Michigan property loss.

Finally, a look across the border to Florida, strictly as contrast. Florida's public-adjuster statute defines a public adjuster as anyone who prepares, completes, or files a claim, or negotiates a settlement, for value, "regardless of how that person describes or presents his or her services." That is Florida's anti-relabeling rule, written into the definition itself. Michigan has no equivalent sentence in twelve twenty two; it reaches relabeling indirectly, through the conditional word-ban we just covered. Florida also gives contractors an explicit safe harbor Michigan lacks: a licensed contractor may discuss or explain a repair bid with the owner or the insurer, as long as they are doing so for the usual and customary fees stated in their own construction contract. Michigan contractors get no comparable sentence, so the boundary gets drawn case by case, through actions like Guldshtadt and decisions like Tredenick.

One practical note before the recap. DIFS contracts its licensing exams to P S I Services L L C. The flat exam fee is forty one dollars, valid one year. The Public Adjuster exam is two hours, one hundred items, seventy one percent to pass. The resident application fee is fifteen dollars plus a five dollar transaction fee, and you have six months from filing to pass the exam or you reapply and pay again. Neither the statute nor DIFS's licensing page mentions continuing education for adjusters, unlike producers, who owe twenty four hours every two years, and neither mentions a surety bond. If a source claims otherwise, it needs a citation, because none was found here.

Recap the numbers. Chapter Twelve runs from twelve hundred through twelve forty seven. Twelve twenty two has exactly five exemptions, none for contractors. Twelve twenty four, subsection four, bars anyone connected with a fire repair contractor from holding the license. Twelve twenty six caps the fee at ten percent and requires the DIFS-approved contract, with the forty-eight-hour, ten-day voidability window. Twelve thirty two conditionally restricts the word "consulting." Twelve forty two gives summary suspension power. Twelve forty four caps civil fines at fifty thousand dollars per order, or one hundred thousand for violating a cease-and-desist order. Guldshtadt lost his license and paid fifty thousand. Tredenick's adjuster lost an eight percent fee over a defective form. Know these numbers and the five exemptions by heart.
